title: U.S national champion Kate Courtney joins FDJ Suez on deal through 2028
content:
United States national champion Kate Courtney has joined FDJ Suez on a contract to the end of 2028.

It is the two-time mountain bike world champion’s first professional deal with a World Tour team — and she signs for the French team after only two road races.

Courtney will now target her home Los Angeles Olympic Games in 2028 and in the meantime is set to compete at this season’s world championships, having earned her spot with a national title in her second-ever road race.

The signing of the 30-year-old is the second major deal FDJ have struck this summer, having given a “historic” contract to former Tour de France Femmes winner and Giro d’Italia champion Demi Vollering in May.

“We want to inspire the next generation, we are really ambitious and we are the number one team in the world,” CEO and team manager Stephen Delcourt told The Athletic.

“When we first had contact with Kate, she wanted to do the maximum on the road. She wanted to target LA28. And for us, it was impossible to miss this opportunity.”

Courtney has spent the majority of her career racing gravel and mountain bike races and earning multiple national and world titles — until she broke her wrist in 2025.

“It caused me to step off the World Cup circuit for a few months, and I raced some marathon events, I learned that I love racing endurance events,” Courtney told The Athletic.

“I loved racing in a team. I loved being able to do multi-day races. Then I learned that the Olympics road course would be a climber’s course in one of my favorite places. And I think together all of those things inspired me to start dreaming about something new.

“FDJ is the team environment that I have been looking for my entire career. And I’m just glad that I kept showing up long enough to have the chance to race with them.”

While the move is unusual, Courtney is not the first member of the World Tour team to have started in a different discipline.

Strade Bianche winner Elise Chabbey started her sporting career as an Olympic canoeist and kayaker, while Amber Kraak competed in European rowing championships before picking up a bike.

Courtney’s 2025 marathon championship win was her second world title on a mountain bike, alongside two national championship triumphs and a cross country world cup in 2019.

After a stage win in the Tour de Feminin in May, her first race in the United States champions jersey with FDJ Suez will be La Périgord Ladies on July 18.

This move has the makings of a fairytale — but it will not be that easy for Courtney.

After winning almost all there is to win on a mountain bike, she is starting from next to nothing on the roads and going full ‘American dream’ for LA28, where the road race will finish overlooking Los Angeles by the Griffin Observatory.

The raw talent is clearly there, as proven by her previous achievements and last month’s national title. But, given the eurocentricity of professional cycling, the real tests are yet to come.

Pauline Ferrand-Prevot was 33 when she won the Tour de France after returning to the roads from her mountain bike career, but unlike Courtney the Frenchwoman had a strong background in both disciplines.

Regardless of how the next few years go, it seems Courtney is in the best place for her new venture — it is an exciting time for FDJ.

They have secured a new contract for leader Demi Vollering — who has been firing on all cylinders in the run-up to the Tour de France Femmes, winning at the Tour of Flanders, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, Flèche Wallonne, Omloop Het Nieuwsblad and the Giro d’Italia this year.

They also have emerging 20-year-old French star Celia Gery on their hands, who just won her first senior national title off the back of a strong performance in the Giro.

This move is a risk, however, and there are no assurances it could pay off. Road racing is a different beast to mountain biking and requires a whole different bike-handling skill set to survive in a packed, ever-faster peloton — while Courtney has indicated that it could be the final years of her career.

If the last few months have taught us anything, though, it is wise to expect the unexpected in the women’s peloton.
